newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bosses, unions agree to split French dole surplus.
newsitem.headline: Bosses, unions agree to split French dole surplus.

text.p: Trade unions and employers agreed on Friday to split a surplus in France's unemployment insurance fund between higher dole payments and a reduction in contributions for workers and employers.

After all-night talks, four of the five unions signed a deal raising basic unemployment benefit from 2,805 francs to 3,100 francs ($590) a month and reducing contributions from 6.60 percent to 6.18 percent of gross wages.
The company's share of wage costs will fall from 4.18 to 3.97 percent and the employee's from 2.42 to 2.21 percent.
The UNEDIC fund, co-managed by unions and the CNPF employers' federation, is forecast to run a surplus of 13 billion francs a year in 1997 and 1998 despite a record jobless rate of 12.6 percent.

Under the accord, which takes effect on January 1 and runs until the end of December 1999, the rate of unemployment benefit which job-seekers receive will dwindle more slowly that before. It will fall every six months instead of every four months.
Unemployed people with 40 years' contributions will be entitled to maximum benefit until they retire.
The employers agreed to extend a system under which workers may take early retirement and be replaced by young recruits.
"This agreement is more than we had believed possible. It's a real triumph," said Michel Jalmain of the Socialist-leaning CFDT union.

"Three-quarters of the surplus will go on employment, to the unemployed but also to workers whose contributions will fall from January 1. The remaining one-quarter will go to reduce employers' contributions," he said.
Only the Communist-led CGT refused to sign the deal, saying it did not give enough to workers and the unemployed.
CGC white-collar union representative Jean-Louis Walter commented: "It's true that it is easier to share out billions than to find savings, as we had to do in previous UNEDIC negotiations."
